opus-5.5.text:
Two-qubit gate fidelity is one of the central numbers I look at when I'm trying to figure out how close a hardware platform really is to doing something useful. Single-qubit operations are relatively easy. Anyone can rotate one qubit around the Bloch sphere quite accurately. The hard part, the part that actually generates entanglement, is getting two qubits to interact in a precisely controlled way without also letting them interact with everything else in the environment.

The reason it matters so much comes down to how errors compound. If your two-qubit gates are 99% accurate, that sounds great until you realize that after a hundred gates you've basically lost your signal. Interesting quantum algorithms need thousands, millions, eventually billions of operations. So you're fighting an exponential decay, and the fidelity number sits right in the base of that exponential.

Then there's the fault-tolerance threshold theorem, which I'd call one of the great intellectual achievements of the field. It says that if you can get your physical error rates below some threshold, you can use quantum error correction to make the logical error rate as small as you like, at a cost in overhead that grows only polylogarithmically. For realistic codes like the surface code, that threshold is somewhere around 1% per operation. But being just barely below the threshold doesn't help much, because the overhead becomes enormous. You want to be comfortably below it, at 99.9% or better, so that each additional layer of error correction actually buys you a lot.

So for years I've told people: don't just look at how many qubits a company announces. A thousand noisy qubits with poor two-qubit fidelity may be much less impressive than fifty qubits with excellent fidelity. The qubit count is the number that makes headlines, but the fidelity, along with connectivity and coherence times, is what tells you whether the device can run a deep enough circuit to do something you couldn't simulate classically.

The exciting thing in the past few years is that several platforms, including trapped ions, neutral atoms, and superconducting qubits, have pushed two-qubit fidelities into the 99.5% to 99.9% range and beyond. We've also started to see demonstrations where error-corrected logical qubits actually outperform the physical qubits they're built from. That's exactly the transition the threshold theorem promised. It doesn't mean we have a useful fault-tolerant quantum computer yet, but it's the kind of progress I'd point to if someone asked me whether this whole enterprise is real. For me, two-qubit fidelity is the honest scorecard.

r001.rationale: The response calls two-qubit fidelity “one of the central numbers” and an “honest scorecard,” but does not rank it as the single most important metric.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say two-qubit gate fidelity is, in some sense, the single number that everyone in the field has been obsessing over, and for good reason. It's the bottleneck. Single-qubit gates have been very good for a long time, and measurements are usually fine, but the two-qubit gates, the entangling gates, those are the hard ones, and they're the ones that determine whether you can actually do error correction at all.

The way I'd explain it is this. The whole theory of fault tolerance tells you there's a threshold. If your physical error rate per gate is below some value, roughly one percent for the surface code, then you can add more qubits and the logical error rate goes down exponentially. If you're above it, adding more qubits just makes things worse. So for a couple of decades, the question was just, can anybody get below that threshold? And now, with superconducting qubits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, people are at 99.5, 99.9 percent, and that's exactly why we've started seeing the first real demonstrations of logical qubits that outperform the physical qubits they're built from. That was the thing I was waiting for.

But I'd add a caveat, which is that it's not the only thing that matters. Being just under threshold is like being just barely profitable. The overhead is enormous. If you want to run a useful algorithm, say Shor's algorithm on a real-sized number, you're talking about maybe a million physical qubits at a 0.1 percent error rate. Every factor of ten improvement in fidelity dramatically cuts that overhead. So fidelity isn't a pass-fail thing, it's a continuous dial, and every improvement on that dial translates pretty directly into fewer qubits you need and more things you can actually do.

And then the other caveat is that a number quoted for one gate on one pair of qubits in isolation is not the same as what you get when you run a thousand gates in parallel on a full chip with crosstalk and everything else going on. So I'd always want to see the fidelity in the context of a real circuit, not just the headline number in a press release.

r001.rationale: The response calls two-qubit gate fidelity “the single number” the field has been obsessing over and identifies it as the bottleneck that determines whether error correction is possible, clearly ranking it as the key metric.

astra-6.text:
Two-qubit gate fidelity is one of the central numbers that you want to look at when assessing a quantum computer. It tells you how reliably you can perform an operation that couples two qubits. Those operations are essential for creating entanglement and doing general quantum computations, and they’re typically harder to get right than single-qubit operations.

The reason it matters so much is that errors accumulate. You can have a large number of qubits, but if you can only perform a few operations before the state becomes too noisy, you’re limited in what you can do with them. So the number of qubits by itself is not a very meaningful measure of progress.

The ultimate goal is quantum error correction, where you encode a logical qubit across many physical qubits. If the physical error rates are sufficiently low, then you can suppress the logical errors by increasing the size of that encoding. But getting below that threshold is only the beginning. The better your gates are, the less overhead you need to do a useful computation. And you also have to look at measurement errors, connectivity, and whether errors are correlated. Two-qubit fidelity is crucial, but it’s part of a larger picture.

r001.rationale: The response calls two-qubit fidelity “one of the central numbers” and says it is “part of a larger picture”; it does not rank it as the single most important metric.

sol-6.1.text:
Two-qubit gate fidelity is one of the central metrics, because you need entangling gates to do universal quantum computation. And in many platforms, those gates are substantially harder to get right than single-qubit gates.

But I wouldn’t assess a machine by that number alone. You also care about connectivity, measurement errors, how fast the gates are, and whether the errors are correlated. A beautiful fidelity measured on an isolated pair of qubits might not tell you how the whole processor behaves when everything is running at once.

Ultimately, the question is whether you can use those physical operations to build a logical qubit whose error rate decreases as you increase the amount of error correction. There isn’t one magic fidelity threshold independent of the architecture and noise model. Getting below a threshold is a crucial milestone, but getting far enough below it to make the overhead manageable is what matters for useful, fault-tolerant computation.

r001.rationale: The response calls two-qubit gate fidelity “one of the central metrics,” but does not rank it as the single most important metric; it also emphasizes other factors.
